question:
Patient note:
A 33-year-old woman, working as a high-school art teacher, was seen late this morning in the combined nephrology–endocrinology clinic at the request of her primary physician to review the trajectory of her renal function and overall medical stability before referral to the regional transplant center. She was diagnosed with autoimmune polyarthritis at age 21 after persistent symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints accompanied by elevated anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies; since that time she has taken methotrexate 25 mg once weekly, folic acid 1 mg daily, and receives a subcutaneous tumor-necrosis-factor inhibitor every other week, with good control of morning stiffness and no recent need for oral glucocorticoid bursts. Two years later, routine screening found a fasting plasma glucose of 198 mg/dL and a glycated hemoglobin of 9.1 %, prompting initiation of basal–bolus insulin; capillary logs over the past month range 110–220 mg/dL before meals despite diligent carbohydrate counting, and last week’s hemoglobin A1c was 8.2 %. Ophthalmology letters document proliferative retinopathy treated with two sessions of pan-retinal photocoagulation six months ago, after which visual acuity stabilized at 20/30 bilaterally; she uses no assistive devices for reading but avoids night driving because of glare. Sensory examination by podiatry three weeks ago revealed diminished vibration at the great toes with intact protective plantar pressure sensation, and she wears custom depth shoes though has never developed an ulcer. Renal indices have shown a progressive rise in serum creatinine from 1.3 mg/dL three years ago to 2.7 mg/dL on last Friday’s comprehensive metabolic panel, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 23 mL/min/1.73 m²; at the same draw, blood urea nitrogen was 48 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, calcium 8.6 mg/dL, phosphorus 5.0 mg/dL, and albumin 3.9 g/dL. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio measured 1,560 mg/g, and an ultrasound last month demonstrated bilaterally normal-sized kidneys with increased cortical echogenicity but no hydronephrosis or stones. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest pressure, palpitations, distal calf cramping while walking, episodic speech difficulty, unilateral weakness, or prior neurologic admissions, and she has no personal history of coronary artery disease (including myocardial infarction), congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular accident or transient ischemic attack, chronic liver disorders (such as hepatitis or cirrhosis), solid-organ or hematologic malignancies, or HIV infection. Her exercise capacity is limited mainly by easy fatigue attributed to anemia of chronic kidney disease (most recent hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 88 fL; ferritin 220 ng/mL), yet she still climbs two flights of classroom stairs daily carrying art supplies without stopping for breath. She has never smoked, drinks a single glass of white wine on holidays, and has no illicit substance use. Family history is notable for a father who started hemodialysis at 59 for diabetic nephropathy and a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis; there is no record of premature coronary disease, stroke, or degenerative dementia among first-degree relatives. Current medications, in addition to those noted, include lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg nightly, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, sevelamer carbonate 800 mg with meals, ergocalciferol 50,000 IU monthly, and a combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation; she reports no drug allergies and avoids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents on nephrology advice. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, cough, wheeze, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, jaundice, melena, hematochezia, dysuria, flank pain, rash outside of occasional metacarpophalangeal erythema, or mood disturbance. On examination she appears well groomed, converses easily, and is oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 144/86 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 82 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, weight 66 kg, height 165 cm, body-mass index 24 kg/m². Carotid upstrokes are brisk with no bruit, jugular venous pressure is 4 cm H₂O, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation with full bilateral breath sounds and no adventitious noises. The abdomen is soft and nontender; the liver edge is not palpable, and there is no splenomegaly or ascites. Extremities show well-healed callus trimming sites over the metatarsal heads, no ulceration or edema, warm skin with intact capillary refill, and palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses graded 2+. Hands exhibit mild ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints with no active synovitis and full passive range of motion. Neurologic screen reveals intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric strength 5/5 throughout, diminished vibration to 64-Hz tuning fork at the halluces, preserved light-touch sensation, normal reflexes, and a steady tandem gait. Laboratory review also demonstrates white-blood-cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 250 × 10⁹/L, international normalized ratio 1.1, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, and total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min, axis within normal limits, PR interval 158 ms, QRS duration 92 ms, and no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment deviation. Doppler echocardiography performed six months ago for hypertension management documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 66 % with concentric remodeling but no regional wall-motion abnormalities or valvular pathology. She seeks clarification regarding the timing of creation of an arteriovenous fistula versus peritoneal catheter, guidance on optimizing insulin dosing now that dietary protein is being liberalized, and advice on whether methotrexate should be withheld as her glomerular filtration rate falls further in anticipation of future transplant listing.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index adds weighted comorbidities. Use the higher weight when a condition has both uncomplicated and complicated categories.
- Age 33: 0 age-adjustment points.
- Rheumatoid arthritis: 1 point for rheumatic disease, even though the arthritis is controlled.
- Diabetes with end-organ damage: 2 points. Proliferative retinopathy establishes this category; do not also count uncomplicated diabetes.
- Moderate to severe chronic kidney disease: 2 points. Her eGFR of 23 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates stage 4 CKD.
- No other qualifying comorbidity is documented: 0 points.
Total = 0 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 5.
Final answer: 5
